item.title: Interior Department announces $450 million in fiscal 2027 Compact funding for Palau, FSM, Marshall Islands
item.description: The U.S. Department of the Interior announced $450 million in fiscal 2027 funding for Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands. The money comes from the Compact of Free Association Amendments Act of 2023, which updated agreements between the U.S. and the three nations.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Department of the Interior announced $450 million in fiscal 2027 funding for Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

The money comes from the Compact of Free Association Amendments Act of 2023, which updated agreements between the U.S. and the three nations.

Palau gets than $41 million to support health care, education, infrastructure projects, the Infrastructure Maintenance Fund and the Fiscal Consolidation Fund.

The Federated States of Micronesia gets $140 million to support health, education, infrastructure, environmental programs, private sector development and capacity building.

The Marshall Islands gets more than $171 million to support payments to Kwajalein landowners, health care, education, environmental programs, capacity building, the U.S. Supplemental Health Fund and improved financial reporting and accountability.

The Republic of the Marshall Islands will also receive $100 million as the final U.S. contribution to its Compact Trust Fund, which supports the nation's long-term fiscal self-reliance.

The Department of the Interior says it will continue to oversee compact assistance to promote accountability, responsible investment and improved public services across the freely associated states.

item.title: GCC announces plans for 50th anniversary celebration
item.description: Guam Community College announced plans for its 50 th anniversary celebration, which begins in January and lasts throughout 2027. The college was established in 1977 with a mission to strengthen career and technical education on Guam.
item.content:encoded:
Guam Community College announced plans for its 50 th anniversary celebration, which begins in January and lasts throughout 2027.

The college was established in 1977 with a mission to strengthen career and technical education on Guam.

During a press conference on Friday, GCC’s leadership said the college is planning activities to bring the community together while supporting student scholarships. These include the workplace giving initiative, the college’s signature Wine Tasting event, Christmas in July and holiday bazaars, a community 5K, a WICHE White Ball gala and a 50 th Anniversary Golf Tournament.

The college is also inviting former VoTech High School and GCC students to reconnect, share their memories, and help tell the stories of the people and experiences that have shaped GCC over the years.

Over the years, GCC has helped thousands of students learn a trade in high school, return to school as an adult, earn a certificate or degree, or continue their education at a four-year university.

“For five decades, this college has helped turn potential into purpose, skills into careers and opportunities into brighter futures,” GCC Interim President Virginia C. Tudela said.

During the announcement, the college’s leadership team said a new mascot will be unveiled as part of the anniversary celebration.

If you are an alumnus and would like to share your story or volunteer to help plan some 50 th Anniversary events, email gcc50@guamcc.edu .

item.title: House passes King-Hinds co-led bill to improve disaster loan information
item.description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. House of Representatives has passed bipartisan legislation co-led by CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds that would require the Small Business Administration to provide more accurate and consistent information to disaster survivors and small businesses seeking federal assistance. The Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act, H.R. 10355, now moves to the Senate for consideration.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. House of Representatives has passed bipartisan legislation co-led by CNMI Delegate Kimberlyn King-Hinds that would require the Small Business Administration to provide more accurate and consistent information to disaster survivors and small businesses seeking federal assistance.

The Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act, H.R. 10355, now moves to the Senate for consideration.

King-Hinds, who co-led the measure with Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., said the bill would help ensure that disaster outreach materials issued by SBA field operations centers reflect current loan terms, eligibility requirements and federal disaster assistance policies.

“In the Northern Mariana Islands, we know firsthand how important timely disaster assistance is,” King-Hinds said, noting that the Commonwealth was struck by two super typhoons earlier this year and many residents and businesses are still recovering.

According to a May 2026 report by the Government Accountability Office, SBA disaster field offices did not consistently update outreach materials, resulting in differing information being provided to disaster survivors. The report found significant variations in how field offices informed applicants that some disaster survivors may qualify for Federal Emergency Management Agency assistance without first applying for an SBA disaster loan.

“Survivors should not receive different answers simply because their disaster is handled by a different SBA field office,” King-Hinds said. “This is a common-sense fix to ensure that disaster survivors get the information they need when they need it most.”

Under the bill, the SBA would be required to establish standardized outreach templates, implement verification procedures before information is released publicly, and conduct annual reviews to ensure consistency across its disaster field operations centers. The agency also would be required to update its procedures after significant policy changes and notify congressional small business committees of those revisions.

Mejia, who introduced the legislation, said the measure was inspired by the challenges small businesses faced following Hurricane Ida in New Jersey.

“When every dollar and every day counts, business owners should never have to navigate outdated or incomplete information from their own government,” Mejia said. “This is a commonsense solution that strengthens government accountability and delivers real results.”

The legislation gained bipartisan backing, including support from Rep. Juan Cisneros, R-Texas, who later joined as a cosponsor.

If enacted, the measure would establish nationwide standards for SBA disaster loan communications, seeking to ensure that disaster survivors receive the same accurate information regardless of which SBA field office handles their case.

item.content:encoded:
KARACHI, Pakistan — In a slum dotted with shimmering pools of sewage, a garment worker nods in recognition as Sydney Sweeney slowly zips up her jeans in an American Eagle Outfitters advertisement playing on a smartphone.

But it's not Sweeney she recognizes — it's the jeans and jacket. This woman, a single mother, has worked on American Eagle production lines and seen those denim styles and similar models. "I know how all of them are made, because I have worked on them," she says.

When Sweeney's advertisement for American Eagle landed in July last year, with the tagline "Sydney Sweeney has great jeans," it triggered debate over whether it was a winking reference to eugenics because of Sweeney's va-va-voom beauty: thin, blonde, blue eyes, large breasts. Following the controversy, American Eagle said in a September 2025 statement that "'Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans' is and always was about the jeans." (Sweeney did not respond to NPR's request for comment.)

Missing from the debate over whether the advertisement was about jeans or genes was any significant reflection on who actually made the American Eagle jeans that Sweeney was wearing — as in, the workers. The majority of garment factories operate out of Asia, so most Americans will never meet the workers making their clothes or see the conditions they're made under.

Workers like that single mother. She asks that we refer to her as S., the initial of her first name, because she fears her bosses at the garment factory where she works will fire her if she's identified. "If you raise your voice, they'll push you out," she says. "We are helpless."

S., a young woman, works at a factory run by a company called Artistic Garment Industries, where she says she's paid about $144 a month, a sum that supports her son and her mother.

She says the factory is "oppressively hot." It was 106 F outside when we met her, and she says the factory inside is even hotter. She says it's hard to leave her workstation to drink water because she has to meet her production targets. She says she has to check the quality of 1,000 to 1,600 pieces of clothing a day — and she's fainted three times this year. "I feel faint, and I can barely stand. I have no energy in my hands and feet," S. says. "They don't even let us sit down." But S. says she has no other options.

Artistic Garment Industries confirmed it makes clothes for American Eagle but tells NPR that it does not push out workers who complain about their working conditions. The company says it has a robust complaints system that workers can use and says it frequently checks on temperatures inside different parts of its factories.

In response to questions NPR sent to American Eagle, the company says it's "committed to working directly with our suppliers to protect the health, safety, and rights of workers. We take the concerns raised by workers — and those whom NPR interviewed — very seriously."

S. is one of around 20 workers we interviewed over the spring and summer in Bangladesh and Pakistan, two of the world's biggest global garment production hubs outside of China. Those men and women worked in five different factories. All of those workers asked NPR not to use their full names and to use only the initial of their first name, worried they'd lose their jobs or be blacklisted from future jobs if they were identified.

Although we focused on the American Eagle jeans worn by Sweeney for the 2025 campaign, the reporting led to a bigger issue: how fast fashion is made, because garment factories make clothes for multiple brands at once. Workers we met told us they made clothes for Levi's, Massimo Dutti, The Gap, H&M and American Eagle. They said it's common knowledge at the factories which brands they are making clothes for, in part because some workers are stitching on the labels.

The garment workers we spoke to offered strikingly similar accounts. And they echoed worker testimonies in multiple reports by labor and climate rights groups. The workers told us they're paid low wages, even as they're expected to reach what they say are unreasonably high production targets, often laboring in sweltering factories.

These are production targets like stitching 200 sleeves an hour or checking the quality of a thousand pieces of clothing a day. The workers we interviewed say they are unable to hydrate or cool down properly, even as extreme heat caused by climate change makes their workplaces and homes even hotter.

It can be four to six degrees hotter inside a factory, says Jason Judd , executive director of the Global Labor Institute at Cornell University, which researched heat inside garment factories and worker homes . "You've got all those bodies, all that material, all that machinery putting off heat. You've got ventilation problems."

"We're starting to see fainting, heat illness, exacerbation of chronic disease, even death," says Cara Schulte, a re searcher at Climate Rights International. She authored two reports on the impacts of heat on garment workers.

Schulte says workers are put under that extreme pressure to reach production targets. A major reason is that brands demand their suppliers make enormous volumes of clothes on tight deadlines and on thin profit margins. And she says garment workers are vulnerable to the heat because they're clustered in countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. She cites U.N. publications stating that t hose factories are "in areas that are warming faster than the global average, that are [already] incredibly hot and humid. "

H&M, one of the brands that workers identified making, said it "put great effort" in ensuring fair payment to its suppliers and that labor costs are "excluded from the price negotiations of our product orders" to ensure that worker wages were not driven down.

Citing her own research, Schulte of Climate Rights International says garment workers are compelled to risk their health to survive. It's not a choice, she says. "Workers are not choosing to take these risks," she says. "They're being forced into them by poverty."

Like a woman who asks we call her R. When we met in February in the Bangladesh capital, Dhaka, R. said she was working six days a week, at least 12 hours a day, for $140 a month at a garment factory run by a company called MBM, which makes denim clothes, including for Levi's. Her job is to stitch 150 pieces of fabric per hour, which are assembled into jeans.

R. says she's considered old for a garment worker — around 40 — and says she's slowing down. She says she's berated by managers who tell her, "Why aren't you speeding up your work?" She says, "If you're short by even a single piece, you face a lot of harassment."

R. says she's managed to meet her targets so far. "Allah has kept me safe," she says. She says friends of hers who could not meet their targets were fired by the company. To reach her targets, R. says, she stays at her station throughout her shift. "Even going to the washroom has become extremely difficult."

So despite Dhaka reaching 98 F this summer, R. says she doesn't drink much water to avoid the need to take bathroom breaks. There's no AC on the factory floor, but R. says managers run ceiling fans and keep windows open.

R. says that if workers feel faint, their bosses will let them rest in a sick room for about 20 minutes. But, she says, management will terminate employment if workers say say they feel sick too often, so she pushes herself to keep going.

MBM did not respond to questions from NPR about worker allegations.

Despite the issues she raised, R. says she works in a good factory. She says the pay is higher than other garment factories. And if she's terminated, she says the company will pay the wages, including overtime, that she's owed. But she doesn't want to be let go.

These garment factories are blazing hot in part because it's expensive to retrofit them with air conditioners. A manager for MBM, who asked that NPR not use their full name because they are not authorized to speak to media, says that the company needs a brand to commit to purchasing long term in order for retrofitting the factory to pay off. The manager says no brand had committed to that kind of long-term business.

Conditions in Bangladesh are still better than in other garment hubs, because of the scrutiny after a building collapse killed more than 1,100 garment workers in 2013. Just three weeks after that disaster, a legally binding commitment called the International Accord emerged between hundreds of brands, companies and trade unions in Bangladesh to protect worker health and safety. So far, 248 global brands and retailers have signed on, covering 2.8 million workers. A version of the International Accord was established in 2023 in Pakistan but has a smaller footprint.

There's meant to be more progress on protecting workers from extreme heat soon. Last December, the International Accord agreed to develop a protocol on heat stress. That means keeping workers cool will be an enforceable commitment for brands. For apparel companies in Bangladesh and Pakistan that have signed on to the accord, the International Accord staff will regularly inspect factories to ensure they're kept cool.

Judd, of the Global Labor Institute, says he believes there will be positive changes because the garment industry knows "they've got a problem — whether it's from a worker rights perspective, or from a business perspective, workers are slowing down, productivity is falling," he says. Either way, "you've got an interest in reducing the heat stress."

But for now, workers in Pakistan , in particular, described sweltering conditions, particularly in the port city of Karachi , one of the world's hottest garment hubs, according to the U.N.'s International Labor Organization.

item.title: New Orleans port sues owners of tanker involved in Mississippi crash
item.description: New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday. The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its ma
item.content:encoded:
New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from people connected to the tanker, which is called Atlantic Asphalt. The lawsuit also names the tanker's owner, Nave Shipping SA and its management company Thome Ship Management as defendants.

The lawsuit states that at 12:30 p.m. Friday, the Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the American Heritage river cruise paddleboat which was docked at the Thalia Street terminal for disembarkment of passengers.

There were almost 200 people on board the American Heritage at the time of the crash, which left the ship on its side and partially submerged. All passengers and crew survived, including more than 100 who were rescued from the river, leading New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno to dub the incident "the miracle on the Mississippi."

There were 32 people brought to the hospital, none with critical injuries.

The port commissioners said as a result of the collision, the Thalia Street terminal had significant damage.

"The extent of said damage remains under investigation, but physical damage is currently estimated to exceed [$1 million], with additional substantial direct, indirect and consequential damages anticipated," the lawsuit reads.

The lawsuit also states that the port expects to incur additional costs, including clean-up, surveys, repair, replacement and salvage costs.

On Friday, port officials requested the tanker be seized and sold to cover costs of the damage. A federal judge approved the seizure request.

Officials claimed that the collision occurred "as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness" by Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping SA and Thome Ship Management.

As of Saturday, eight people remained in the hospital, two in serious condition.

Mayor Moreno said Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed away from the site, but noted it could take weeks to fully remove the American Heritage.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said that operations were now focused on fully reopening the river and safe removal of hazardous material on board the American Heritage. Burnham said it is estimated there are 160,000 gallons of fuel on board the ship.

"We're going to have divers in the water so they can do a full assessment on what's the right path to be able to remove it," Burnham said. "We also have teams that have been deployed throughout the entire area, the river system to monitor the area for any pollution."

Burnham said there are restrictions in place for boat traffic along the Mississippi River.

The exact cause of the crash is unknown, though Burnham said the tanker appeared to have an issue with steering. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

John DeLeeuw, board member with the NTSB, said during a Saturday briefing that the tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered.

"The voyage data recorder essentially is going to provide the data," DeLeeuw said. "It's like a flight data recorder on an aircraft. We can look at speeds and all kinds of information. It's essentially covering speed all kinds of maneuverings that was done on the ship."

A preliminary report by the NTSB is expected within 30 days, with the final report on probable causes and safety recommendations coming in 18 to 24 months.

item.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
item.description: The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures. Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years . The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years .
item.content:encoded:
The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.

Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years . The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years .

The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.

Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18 . The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided .

So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.

The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.

The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.

The president of their rival organization , Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."

Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."

In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.

One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program , which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.

In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.

Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures . (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans .)

In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.

Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.

Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.

North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.

In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.

That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

Colin Campbell of WUNC, Sarah Kallis of Georgia Public Broadcasting, Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of WHYY and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ, contributed to this story.

item.title: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
item.description: Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly. It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.
item.content:encoded:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.

"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."

A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.

Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.

"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.

There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.

When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.

"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.

Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.

"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."

According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.

But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.

In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.

Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.

Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center , said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."

"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."

But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.

The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.

Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.

Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.

Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.

Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.

"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.

The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."

"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.

"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."

In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.

It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.

Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress , a left-leaning think tank.
